entry.evidence: So it remains to be discussed whether the eddy growth is not suppressed in weak jet months

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF with publisher XML text (abstract and captions)

steps.action: The authors take from Nakamura (1992) the observation that the midwinter suppression of the NPST is strong aloft and weak at the surface.
steps.quote: the midwinter suppression of North Pacific storm tracks (NPSTs) is more pronounced in the upper troposphere but barely evident at the surface

steps.action: They list three published strong-jet mechanisms for the suppression: short residence time, the barotropic governor, and the subtropical-jet regime.
steps.quote: The suppression effect of a strong jet is mainly contributed by three of its features

steps.action: They ask whether eddy growth is also suppressed in weak-jet months, noting that an Eulerian minimum mixes eddy number with eddy growth.
steps.quote: it remains to be discussed whether the eddy growth is not suppressed in weak jet months

steps.action: Citing Okajima et al. (2022), they narrow the question to the generation-to-lysis growth process, compared between upper-level and lower-level eddies.
steps.quote: many previous studies have not focused on their specific growth process

steps.action: They take 6-hourly winds, temperature and geopotential height for 1979–2019 from the NCEP–DOE AMIP-II reanalysis.
steps.quote: The data used in this study are from the NCEP–DOE AMIP-II reanalysis dataset

steps.action: They set up TRACK on 200 and 850 hPa relative vorticity (threshold 1.0e-5, lifetime over 2 days, displacement over 10°, tracks must pass 30°N), compute Hodges (1996) density statistics and mean growth rate, and use 10-day high-pass EKE as the Eulerian metric.
steps.quote: The relative vorticity was first calculated from the 41 years of wind (u, v) fields and used as a tracking object

steps.action: They split the cold-season months into 110 strong-jet months (index above 55 m/s, almost all in winter) and 119 weak-jet months (index below 50 m/s).
steps.quote: All results shown below are divided into two groups based on the jet index during 40 consecutive cold seasons

steps.action: They correlate the jet index with baroclinicity (r=0.78), with 850 hPa EKE (r=0.5) and with 200 hPa EKE (r=−0.6), to justify the grouping and to show the opposite responses of the two levels.
steps.quote: indicate the suitability of the grouping for analyzing the response of NPSTs to the jet/baroclinicity

steps.action: They compare 850 hPa EKE and track density in the two composites with the baroclinic zone and find them consistent with linear baroclinic instability theory.
steps.quote: All these features are consistent with linear baroclinic instability theory

steps.action: They show that 200 hPa EKE and track density fall and shift south in strong-jet months, opposite to the lower level and consistent with Hoskins and Hodges (2019).
steps.quote: the upper-level NPST shows a pattern of variation opposite to that of the lower-level NPST

steps.action: They map 850 hPa genesis and lysis density: lower-level eddies form in East Asia and the Northwest Pacific, where baroclinicity is high, and their numbers follow baroclinicity.
steps.quote: the lower-level eddies that affect the North Pacific are mainly generated in East Asia

steps.action: They map 200 hPa genesis and lysis density: in strong-jet months genesis drops sharply northwest of the jet core and rises northeast of it, and eddies formed upstream die before 150°E.
steps.quote: the number of active upper-level eddies generated on the northwest side of the jet core decreases drastically during the strong jet months

steps.action: They set the drop in upper-level eddy number against Hadas and Kaspi (2021), with which it agrees, adding regional detail that study lacked.
steps.quote: is consistent with the findings presented by Hadas and Kaspi (2021)

steps.action: They reject reduced upstream seeding from Asia (Penny et al. 2010) as the main cause of fewer Northwest Pacific disturbances and attribute the drop to reduced local genesis.
steps.quote: it seems to have little to do with the decline in upstream seeds

steps.action: They compare weak-jet months and find that upper-level eddies upstream of the jet core fail to grow even then, so the suppression lasts the whole cold season.
steps.quote: [...] of growth of the upper-level eddies upstream of the jet core holds even in weak jet months

steps.action: They compute the genesis density of eddies that die in two lysis boxes and confirm that these eddies came from the northern Pacific jet (result not shown).
steps.quote: We have calculated the genesis density of the eddies that died out

steps.action: They map mean growth rate: lower-level growth sits in the baroclinic zone and rises with baroclinicity, while upper-level growth lies near the jet exit, outside the baroclinic zone.
steps.quote: the main growth area of the lower-level eddies is located just in the baroclinic zone

steps.action: They use the growth-rate diagnostic as an independent check on the genesis and lysis conclusion for upper-level eddies.
steps.quote: This again validates the conclusion about the upper-level eddy growth process shown in Fig. 3

steps.action: They limit where growth rates can be trusted: low confidence where track density is low (Mongolia), credible inside the North Pacific storm track.
steps.quote: our confidence in the estimated mean growth rate in and around Mongolia will be low

steps.action: They keep the contrast: lower-level eddies follow linear baroclinic theory, while upper-level genesis and growth are governed by jet position, with suppression upstream of the jet core.
steps.quote: The activity of lower-level eddies is highly consistent with the theory of linear baroclinic instability

steps.action: They propose, without testing it, that energy advection and dispersion control upper-level eddy growth, and defer the vertical-coupling explanation to future work.
steps.quote: we can still speculate that the energy advection and dispersion may play an important role in the upper-level eddy growth

No; eddy genesis and growth are diagnosed by tracking vorticity in reanalysis fields

Only implicitly: linear baroclinic theory predicts growth that rises with baroclinicity
Conditions found: jet-strength composites built from reanalysis months

end.claim: In 1979–2019 cold-season NCEP–DOE reanalysis, lower-level eddy genesis and growth coincide with the baroclinic zone and increase with baroclinicity; upper-level eddies generated upstream of the Pacific jet core fail to grow throughout the cold season, and a stronger jet suppresses Northwest Pacific genesis while favouring genesis near the jet exit.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the Lagrangian genesis and lysis density maps at 200 hPa, split by jet-strength composite, the authors could not have shown that upstream upper-level eddies fail to grow even in weak-jet months.

gates.evidence: All data are existing reanalysis fields; no stated hypothesis directed their acquisition. The lower-level result was set against linear baroclinic instability theory and could have failed it (p. 2, p. 5). The upper-level findings are descriptive composites, and no significance test is reported. Tracking thresholds follow Hoskins and Hodges (2002), but the jet-index thresholds and composite regions are not stated as fixed before the analysis.

novelty_claims.quote: The novelty of this paper is the emphasis on the specific eddy growth process
further revealing the discrepancy between the upper- and lower-level [...]

limits: Locations: the supplied XML text contains only the abstract and figure captions, so all body-text quotes and locations come from PDF pages. Robustness: one reanalysis (NCEP–DOE R-2, 2.5°) is used; tracking thresholds, the jet-index cutoffs (55 and 50 m/s) and the averaging regions are not varied; one check is reported as 'not shown'. Statistics: the word 'significantly' is used for composite differences (p. 2), but no significance test is described (inference: none was performed or reported). Sub-claims and their status: the lower-level consistency with linear baroclinic theory is a regularity_in_range; the rejection of reduced upstream seeding (contra Penny et al. 2010) is best_explanation and is hedged ('seems'); the energy advection and dispersion mechanism is an untested hypothesis (status none). Review: two reviewers are thanked, but no review file was supplied, so changes forced by review cannot be identified. Process: why only cold-season months were used, and how the regions were chosen, is not stated.

disagreements.target: Strong-jet suppression literature based on the Eulerian midwinter minimum (Nakamura 1992; Chang 2001; Harnik and Chang 2004; Yuval et al. [...]
disagreements.support: Tracking shows that upper-level eddies upstream of the jet core fail to grow in weak-jet months as well, so suppression is not confined to midwinter.
disagreements.quote: the midwinter minimum of the NPST in an Eulerian framework does not mean that the eddy growth is suppressed only in midwinter

disagreements.target: Surface-cyclone tracking studies (Schemm and Schneider 2018; Schemm et al. 2021)
disagreements.support: Argued from Okajima et al. (2022): upper- and lower-level eddies grow inconsistently in winter, so surface cyclones cannot reveal the suppression.
disagreements.quote: focusing on the surface cyclones does not provide any useful insights into understanding the midwinter suppression phenomenon

disagreements.target: Penny et al. (2010): reduced frequency of disturbances entering the Pacific from midlatitude Asia in winter
disagreements.support: The 200 hPa genesis density composites attribute the drop in Northwest Pacific disturbances to reduced local genesis.
disagreements.quote: it seems to have little to do with the decline in upstream seeds

disagreements.target: Hadas and Kaspi (2021): fewer upper-level eddies under strong jets
disagreements.support: The overall drop is confirmed, but genesis increases northeast of the jet core in strong-jet months, a regional detail they did not analyse.
disagreements.quote: but they did not analyze the regional details

disagreements.target: Previous studies concentrating on NPST strength
disagreements.support: The authors argue that the eddy growth process, not Eulerian storm-track strength, is the quantity that matches linear baroclinic theory.
disagreements.quote: most previous studies have concentrated on the NPST strength, which does not exactly match the physical processes depicted by the baroclinicity

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Accounting for the long-term weakening of the midwinter suppression after the late 1980s
alternatives_considered.reason: The climatological seasonality has not changed much since the late 1980s

alternatives_considered.chosen: EKE as the Eulerian metric, plus mean growth rate from tracks
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 'Accumulated eddy activity' (track density times mean intensity; Guo et al. 2017)
alternatives_considered.reason: To provide information about mean intensity from the perspective of eddy growth

alternatives_considered.alternatives: LAGRANTO (Wernli and Davies 1997; Sprenger and Wernli 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (TRACK was provided by K. Hodges)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Strong-jet months with index above 55 m/s; weak-jet months with index below 50 m/s
alternatives_considered.alternatives: The commonly used strong-jet threshold of 45 m/s
alternatives_considered.reason: Months with jet index above 55 m/s are almost all in winter, which allows a winter-versus-autumn/spring contrast
